newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Teva eyes European generics market.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Teva eyes European generics market.

text.p: Teva Pharmaceutical Industries says it has found the formula for competing in a difficult U.S. generic drugs market and is building a European operation it hopes will replicate it.
"We think the European generics market will develop in the same direction as the U.S. market," Dan Suesskind, Teva's chief financial officer, told Reuters.

In the past year, Teva has acquired companies in Hungary, Italy and Britain, and in the third quarter European sales accounted for the first time for a significant portion of Teva's total revenues -- $43 million, or 18 percent of the total.

Teva's European drive comes as the Israeli company faces a consolidation in the U.S. generics market, where it has emerged as the second-biggest competitor with its acquisition of Biocraft Laboratories last May. U.S. sales account for half of Teva's total.

Price erosion due to increased competition and market share battles in the U.S. generics market left Teva's U.S. revenues unchanged for the third quarter compared to a year earlier. But the company was able to boost gross margins 3.1 percentage points to 39 percent company-wide by bringing out new, high-margin generic products.
Suesskind said Teva had other generic drugs in the pipeline that would enable it to continue to reap benefits from new-product introductions for the foreseeable future.

Lehman Brothers analyst Richard Silver agrees. "Although overall generic pricing remains a risk for the foreseeable future, we believe that Teva's two new products in the U.S. ...will be large earnings contributors in fourth-quarter 1996 and into 1997," he wrote in a recent report.
At least one major competitor, IVAX Corp., is hoping to cut costs by merging with a pharmaceutical distributor Bergen Brunswig.

Even though Teva expects to wring annual savings of $15 million from its merger with Biocraft, Suesskind says he does not understand what the Ivax-Bergen combination will yield for the two companies and expresses no competitive concerns.
As to further mergers or acquisitions in the United States, he said: "At the moment we have no plans."
Ultimately, Suesskind sees Teva exploiting synergies from its European and U.S. businesses. "We can use certain (drug) filings approved in the United States also in Europe," he said.
Another major factor in Teva's earnings outlook is its first-ever proprietary drug, a multiple sclerosis treatment called Copaxone.

The company received preliminary approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in October and Lehman expects Teva will get full approval by year end. Societe Generale says Copaxone alone should boost Teva's earnings by $0.50-$0.80 a share in 1998 on sales of $65 million-100 million.
In 1995, Teva's total revenues were $811.2 million, yielding earnings of $1.15 per American depositary receipt.
